--- title: "Row & Column Verbs" subtitle: "≈ dplyr single-table verbs: `filter()` · `arrange()` · `distinct()` · `slice_*()` · `select()` · `rename()` · `relocate()`" jupyter: python3 --- R4DS's *Data transformation* chapter teaches dplyr's single-table verbs on `flights`. This chapter follows the same path in Polars. The one-line translations are in the cheatsheet; this chapter covers the defaults that differ: where nulls go, which row survives a tie, what order rows come back in, and which column verbs change a frame in place. ## In tidyverse {#sec-verb-tidyverse} ```r library(dplyr) library(nycflights13) flights |> filter(dep_delay > 120, month == 1) flights |> arrange(month, day, desc(dep_delay)) flights |> distinct(origin, dest, .keep_all = TRUE) flights |> slice_max(distance, n = 3) # 342 rows: ties are kept flights |> slice_sample(prop = 1) # every row, shuffled flights |> select(year:day, tail_num = tailnum) flights |> relocate(starts_with("arr"), .before = dep_time) ``` dplyr makes promises about order and ties without being asked: 1. `arrange()` keeps tied rows in input order and puts `NA` last, in both directions. 2. `filter()` and `distinct()` keep rows in input order; `distinct()` keeps the first copy. 3. `slice_max()` and `slice_min()` keep ties. Polars keeps `filter()`'s order and makes the rest opt-in. The docstrings give the reason: preserving order "is more expensive to compute", and leaving the choice of row open "allows more optimizations". ## Mental model {#sec-verb-model} ```text ROW VERBS: change the height, never touch a column order of the result ───────────────────────────────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────────────── by predicate filter(p) remove(p) input order by position head tail slice gather gather_every input order (by definition) by value sort(by) tied rows: input order only with maintain_order=True top_k(k, by) bottom_k(k, by) exactly k rows; ties broken arbitrarily by identity unique(subset, keep) arbitrary unless maintain_order=True by chance sample(n | fraction, seed) arbitrary unless shuffle=True / False COLUMN VERBS: change the width, never touch a row ───────────────────────────────────────────────── select drop rename with_columns with_row_index return a new frame insert_column df.columns = [...] modify the frame in place (!) ``` Read the right-hand column as the contract. Anything marked "arbitrary" can differ between runs, and the fix is always an explicit argument (@sec-verb-gotchas). ## Mechanics {#sec-verb-mechanics} ::: {#cf842470 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs from pl_notes import datasets flights_df = datasets.flights() # 336,776 × 19, as nycflights13::flights penguins_df = datasets.penguins() ``` ::: ### Filter rows {#sec-verb-filter} Comma-separated predicates are combined with AND, as in dplyr. Equality tests also have a keyword shorthand: each `name=value` becomes `pl.col(name) == value`. In R, `filter(month = 1)` is the classic typo that dplyr rejects; in Polars it is valid: ::: {#d48f452f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 120, month=1, origin="JFK").select( "month", "day", "origin", "dest", "dep_delay" ).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 5)
monthdayorigindestdep_delay
i64i64strstri64
11"JFK""BWI"853
11"JFK""SJU"122
11"JFK""LAX"131
``` ::: ::: The shorthand is only `==`. `origin=["JFK", "LGA"]` raises (use `pl.col("origin").is_in(...)`), and `tailnum=None` compares with null, so it keeps no rows (Polars warns). **Nulls drop the row.** A row is kept only where the predicate is `true`; `false` and null both drop it, as in dplyr. So `filter(p)` and `filter(~p)` do not add up to the whole frame: rows where `p` is null are in neither. `remove(p)` is the exact complement of `filter(p)`. It drops the rows where `p` is `true` and keeps everything else, nulls included: ::: {#75aeb91a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} late = pl.col("dep_delay") > 0 { "filter(late)": flights_df.filter(late).height, "filter(~late)": flights_df.filter(~late).height, "remove(late)": flights_df.remove(late).height, # ~late plus the null rows "all rows": flights_df.height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {'filter(late)': 128432, 'filter(~late)': 200089, 'remove(late)': 208344, 'all rows': 336776} ``` ::: ::: The 8,255 cancelled flights (null `dep_delay`) are only in `remove()`. In dplyr the same complement is `filter(!(dep_delay > 0) | is.na(dep_delay))`. Grouped filters such as `filter(n() > 1000, .by = dest)` are window expressions: `pl.len().over("dest") > 1000` (see [Window Functions](window.qmd)). ### Sort rows {#sec-verb-sort} `sort()` takes several keys. `descending=` and `nulls_last=` each take one bool for all keys, or a list with one bool per key; a list of the wrong length raises a `ValueError`. This is `arrange(month, day, desc(dep_delay))` with `NA` last: ::: {#430a2475 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.sort( "month", "day", "dep_delay", descending=[False, False, True], nulls_last=True, ).select("month", "day", "dep_delay", "carrier", "flight").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 5)
monthdaydep_delaycarrierflight
i64i64i64stri64
11853"MQ"3944
11379"EV"4321
11290"EV"4417
``` ::: ::: Without `nulls_last=True`, nulls come first in both directions (@sec-verb-nulls-first). Keys can also be expressions ([Expressions & Contexts](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-contexts)). **What "sorted" means for each dtype.** Numbers and dates sort by value. Strings sort by code point: digits before letters, every uppercase letter before every lowercase one, `"10"` before `"9"`. That matches `arrange()` in dplyr ≥ 1.1, which uses the C locale by default (base R's `sort()` uses the system locale). A `Categorical` sorts by its strings; an `Enum` sorts by its level order, like a factor: ::: {#de72a57a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} words = pl.Series(["banana", "Apple", "apple", "Banana", "10", "9"]) { "String": words.sort().to_list(), "Categorical": words.cast(pl.Categorical).sort().to_list(), "Enum": words.cast(pl.Enum(["9", "10", "apple", "Apple", "banana", "Banana"])).sort().to_list(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` {'String': ['10', '9', 'Apple', 'Banana', 'apple', 'banana'], 'Categorical': ['10', '9', 'Apple', 'Banana', 'apple', 'banana'], 'Enum': ['9', '10', 'apple', 'Apple', 'banana', 'Banana']} ``` ::: ::: For a case-insensitive order, sort by an expression: `sort(pl.col("word").str.to_lowercase())`. ### Distinct rows {#sec-verb-unique} `unique(subset=...)` decides what a duplicate is from the `subset` columns but always returns **every** column: it is `distinct(..., .keep_all = TRUE)`. For `distinct(origin, dest)`, which keeps only those two, select first: `select("origin", "dest").unique()`. `keep=` chooses which copy survives: ::: {#0e716b7e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} sightings_df = pl.DataFrame({ "tailnum": ["N1", "N2", "N1", "N3", "N2", "N1"], "seen": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], }) { keep: sightings_df.unique("tailnum", keep=keep, maintain_order=True).rows() for keep in ["first", "last", "none", "any"] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` {'first': [('N1', 1), ('N2', 2), ('N3', 4)], 'last': [('N3', 4), ('N2', 5), ('N1', 6)], 'none': [('N3', 4)], 'any': [('N1', 1), ('N2', 2), ('N3', 4)]} ``` ::: ::: - `"first"` is `distinct(.keep_all = TRUE)`. - `"last"` keeps the last copy, and `maintain_order=True` orders rows by where that copy sat: `N3` (row 4), `N2` (row 5), `N1` (row 6). - `"none"` drops every repeated key (≈ `filter(n() == 1, .by = tailnum)`). - `"any"`, the **default**, promises nothing about which copy survives. Here it picked the first ones; don't rely on that (@sec-verb-unique-defaults). Null keys count as equal to each other, as in `distinct()`. `subset=` also accepts expressions, so you can deduplicate on a computed key without adding it as a column. The first penguin in each 1 kg mass band, the null band included: ::: {#ad6bb5f5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.unique( subset=(pl.col("body_mass_g") / 1000).floor(), keep="first", maintain_order=True ).select("species", "island", "body_mass_g") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
shape: (6, 3)
speciesislandbody_mass_g
strstri64
"Adelie""Torgersen"3750
"Adelie""Torgersen"null
"Adelie""Torgersen"4675
"Adelie""Dream"2975
"Gentoo""Biscoe"5700
"Gentoo""Biscoe"6300
``` ::: ::: (The integer key `pl.col("body_mass_g") // 1000` would be more natural, but as a `subset=` it panics in Polars 2.0.0, an engine bug. `// pl.lit(1000, dtype=pl.Int64)` works.) **Flag instead of filter.** Four expressions mark duplicates without removing them: ::: {#908df1d4 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} sightings_df.with_columns( is_duplicated=pl.col("tailnum").is_duplicated(), # every copy of a repeated key is_first_distinct=pl.col("tailnum").is_first_distinct(), # !duplicated(tailnum) is_last_distinct=pl.col("tailnum").is_last_distinct(), # !duplicated(tailnum, fromLast = TRUE) is_unique=pl.col("tailnum").is_unique(), # keys seen exactly once ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
shape: (6, 6)
tailnumseenis_duplicatedis_first_distinctis_last_distinctis_unique
stri64boolboolboolbool
"N1"1truetruefalsefalse
"N2"2truetruefalsefalse
"N1"3truefalsefalsefalse
"N3"4falsetruetruetrue
"N2"5truefalsetruefalse
"N1"6truefalsetruefalse
``` ::: ::: For a key of several columns, wrap them in a struct: `pl.struct("origin", "dest").is_first_distinct()`. `df.is_duplicated()` flags whole-row duplicates. **Counting** (≈ `n_distinct()`): `flights_df.n_unique(subset=["origin", "dest"])` returns a Python `int` (224 routes); the expression `pl.col("dest").n_unique()` works in any context; `approx_n_unique()` estimates with HyperLogLog++ when an exact count is too expensive. ### Rows by position {#sec-verb-slice} Positions are 0-based, and a negative position counts from the end. That is Python's convention, not R's: in R a negative index **drops** rows. In `slice(offset, length)`, a negative offset starts from the end, a negative length stops that many rows before the end, and no length runs to the end: ::: {#c7751727 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} positions_df = pl.DataFrame({"i": range(10)}) { "slice(2, 3)": positions_df.slice(2, 3)["i"].to_list(), # slice(3:5) "slice(-3)": positions_df.slice(-3)["i"].to_list(), # slice_tail(n = 3) "slice(2, -3)": positions_df.slice(2, -3)["i"].to_list(), "slice(8, 5)": positions_df.slice(8, 5)["i"].to_list(), # past the end: clipped "head(-3)": positions_df.head(-3)["i"].to_list(), # slice_head(n = -3) "tail(-3)": positions_df.tail(-3)["i"].to_list(), # slice_tail(n = -3) "gather([0, 3, -1])": positions_df.gather([0, 3, -1])["i"].to_list(), # slice(c(1, 4, n())) "gather_every(3)": positions_df.gather_every(3)["i"].to_list(), # every 3rd row } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` {'slice(2, 3)': [2, 3, 4], 'slice(-3)': [7, 8, 9], 'slice(2, -3)': [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 'slice(8, 5)': [8, 9], 'head(-3)': [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 'tail(-3)': [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], 'gather([0, 3, -1])': [0, 3, 9], 'gather_every(3)': [0, 3, 6, 9]} ``` ::: ::: `slice()` clips silently, but `gather()` (≈ `slice()` with a vector of positions) is strict. dplyr silently ignores positions past the end; `gather()` raises, and `null_on_oob=True` returns a row of nulls instead: ::: {#30ee07f1 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} positions_df.gather([1, 10]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
OutOfBoundsError: gather indices are out of bounds
``` ::: ::: ::: Square brackets do the same jobs: `df[2:5]` is `slice(2, 3)`, `df[[0, 3]]` is `gather([0, 3])`. The methods chain, and they also work on a `LazyFrame`. ### Rows by value: `top_k()` and `bottom_k()` {#sec-verb-topk} `top_k(k, by=)` returns the *k* rows with the largest `by` values; `bottom_k()` the smallest. Several keys are compared like a multi-key sort, and `reverse=` (one bool, or one per key) flips a key's direction. The longest flights, ties broken by the largest departure delay: ::: {#24b5c7b4 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.top_k(3, by=["distance", "dep_delay"]).select( "origin", "dest", "distance", "dep_delay" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
origindestdistancedep_delay
strstri64i64
"JFK""HNL"49831301
"JFK""HNL"4983206
"JFK""HNL"4983186
``` ::: ::: (The most delayed flight of 2013 was the 1,301-minute departure to Honolulu.) Unlike `sort()`, both verbs rank nulls below every value, so `top_k(3)` and `sort(descending=True).head(3)` disagree on a column with nulls. Two more differences from `slice_max()`: exactly *k* rows come back, and the docstring promises no output order (@sec-verb-ties). ### Random rows: `sample()` {#sec-verb-sample} `sample()` takes `n` or `fraction` (which rounds down: 0.02 × 344 rows gives 6), `with_replacement=False`, `seed=` (without one, every render draws a different sample) and `shuffle=`. The last one is the surprise. Its default, `None`, promises no order, and in practice a sample of every row comes back in input order. `slice_sample(prop = 1)` shuffles; here you need `shuffle=True`: ::: {#b3b845f3 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df_indexed = penguins_df.with_row_index("row") { "fraction=1": penguins_df_indexed.sample(fraction=1, seed=42)["row"].head(5).to_list(), "fraction=1, shuffle=True": penguins_df_indexed.sample( fraction=1, shuffle=True, seed=42 )["row"].head(5).to_list(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` {'fraction=1': [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], 'fraction=1, shuffle=True': [201, 17, 247, 27, 145]} ``` ::: ::: dplyr's `slice_sample(n = 400)` on 344 rows silently returns 344. Polars raises unless `with_replacement=True`: ::: {#2646900a .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.sample(400, seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ShapeError: cannot take a larger sample than the total population when `with_replacement=false`
``` ::: ::: ::: `sample()` is eager-only: `LazyFrame` has no `sample()` method. ### Per-group slices {#sec-verb-groups} `group_by(g, maintain_order=True).head(n)` and `.tail(n)` are `slice_head()` / `slice_tail()` with `by =`. Every other per-group slice is a window predicate in `filter()`, which keeps rows in input order. This is `slice_max(body_mass_g, n = 2, by = species, with_ties = FALSE)`: ::: {#811cbc14 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.filter( pl.col("body_mass_g").rank("ordinal", descending=True).over("species") <= 2 ).select("species", "island", "body_mass_g") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
shape: (6, 3)
speciesislandbody_mass_g
strstri64
"Adelie""Biscoe"4725
"Adelie""Biscoe"4775
"Gentoo""Biscoe"6300
"Gentoo""Biscoe"6050
"Chinstrap""Dream"4550
"Chinstrap""Dream"4800
``` ::: ::: `"ordinal"` breaks ties by position; `"min"` keeps them. A random 2 per group shuffles a row counter: `pl.int_range(pl.len()).shuffle(seed=1).over("species") < 2`. More in [Window Functions](window.qmd) and [Grouping & Aggregation](group-agg.qmd). ### Select, drop, rename {#sec-verb-select} The cheatsheet maps most of tidyselect ([Select Columns](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-select)). The column range `year:day` has no verb; on a `DataFrame` a label slice with square brackets does it, inclusive at both ends: ::: {#f0bffef5 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} year_to_day = flights_df[:, "year":"day"].columns year_to_day, flights_df.drop(year_to_day).columns[:3] # year:day and !year:day ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` (['year', 'month', 'day'], ['dep_time', 'sched_dep_time', 'dep_delay']) ``` ::: ::: On a `LazyFrame`, select by position instead: `cs.by_index(range(0, 3))`. **`drop()` is strict.** A name that doesn't exist raises, which catches typos. `strict=False` ignores missing names (≈ `select(-any_of(...))`), and a selector that matches nothing never raises: ::: {#9896b88c .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.drop("tail_num") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ColumnNotFoundError: "tail_num" not found
``` ::: ::: ::: **`rename()` takes `{old: new}`**, the reverse of dplyr's `new = old`, or a function `str → str` applied to every name. Renamed columns keep their position, and all renames happen at once, so a swap works: ::: {#885760a4 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select("origin", "dest").head(2).rename({"origin": "dest", "dest": "origin"}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
destorigin
strstr
"EWR""IAH"
"LGA""IAH"
``` ::: ::: An old name that doesn't exist raises unless `strict=False`. A new name that already exists (and isn't being renamed away) raises a `DuplicateError`. To rename only some columns with a function (≈ `rename_with(.cols = )`), see [Selectors](../core/selectors.qmd#sec-sel-recipes). ### Reorder columns {#sec-verb-relocate} There is no `relocate()`. Moving columns to the front or back is a `select()` of the moved columns plus everything else. With selectors, "everything else" is the complement `~` ([Set algebra](../core/selectors.qmd#sec-sel-algebra)): ::: {#f1ca4f46 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select(cs.starts_with("arr"), ~cs.starts_with("arr")).columns[:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` ['arr_time', 'arr_delay', 'year', 'month'] ``` ::: ::: To **create** a column at the front (≈ `mutate(.before = 1)`), pass the new expression before `pl.all()`. There is no name clash, because the name is new: ::: {#6daee92e .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select( (pl.col("dep_delay") - pl.col("arr_delay")).alias("gain"), pl.all() ).columns[:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` ['gain', 'year', 'month', 'day'] ``` ::: ::: `.before =` / `.after =` another column needs the name list built in Python (@sec-verb-recipes). ### Add, replace and index columns {#sec-verb-mutate} `with_columns()` places each output by name. An existing name is replaced **in its position**; a new name is appended at the end, in argument order (keyword arguments come last, see [Naming](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-naming)): ::: {#7ab4bf9f .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select("year", "month", "day", "air_time").head(2).with_columns( hours=pl.col("air_time") / 60, # new name → appended month=pl.col("month").cast(pl.Int8), # existing name → replaced in place ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 5)
yearmonthdayair_timehours
i64i8i64i64f64
2013112273.783333
2013112273.783333
``` ::: ::: dplyr's `.keep =` argument has no Polars equivalent, but an expression knows its inputs (`meta.root_names()`), which is enough to rebuild `mutate(gain = dep_delay - arr_delay, .keep = "used")`: ::: {#567ec8e6 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} gain = pl.col("dep_delay") - pl.col("arr_delay") flights_df.select(*gain.meta.root_names(), gain=gain).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 3)
dep_delayarr_delaygain
i64i64i64
211-9
420-16
233-31
``` ::: ::: `.keep = "none"` is plain `select()`; `.keep = "unused"` is `with_columns(gain=gain).drop(gain.meta.root_names())`. And `with_columns_seq()` is not dplyr's sequential `mutate()`: it runs expressions one after another instead of in parallel, but a later one still can't see an earlier one's output. `with_row_index()` (≈ `rowid_to_column()`) adds the index as the **first** column, named `index` by default, with dtype `UInt32` (unsigned, see [Counts are unsigned](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-unsigned)). `offset=` sets the starting number and must not be negative: ::: {#f141d301 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.with_row_index("id", offset=1).select("id", "species").head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
idspecies
u32str
1"Adelie"
2"Adelie"
``` ::: ::: ## Where it bites {#sec-verb-gotchas} | tidyverse behaviour | Polars behaviour | |---|---| | `arrange()` puts `NA` last | `sort()` puts nulls first, even with `descending=True`; pass `nulls_last=True` | | `arrange()` keeps tied rows in input order | multi-key `sort()` does not; pass `maintain_order=True` | | `slice_max()` keeps ties | `top_k()` returns *k* arbitrary rows among ties | | `distinct()` keeps the first copy, in input order | `unique()` keeps any copy, in an order that changes every call | | `distinct(x)` drops the other columns | `unique(subset="x")` keeps them | | `slice(-1)` drops the first row | `slice(-1)` is the last row | | `slice()` ignores positions past the end | `gather()` raises; `null_on_oob=True` gives a null row | | `slice_sample(n = 400)` on 344 rows returns 344 | `sample(400)` raises; pass `with_replacement=True` | | `slice_sample(prop = 1)` shuffles | `sample(fraction=1)` keeps input order unless `shuffle=True` | | `filter(month = 1)` is an error | `filter(month=1)` means `pl.col("month") == 1` | | `select(x, everything())` moves `x` first | duplicate output names raise | | `slice_head(n = 1, by = g)` keeps column order | `group_by("g").head(1)` moves `g` to the front | | `names(df) <- ...` modifies a copy | `df.columns = ...` and `insert_column()` modify in place | : The differences at a glance {.striped} ### Nulls sort first, even descending {#sec-verb-nulls-first} R4DS's `arrange(desc(dep_delay))` shows the most delayed flights. The same call in Polars shows cancelled ones: ::: {#d1694bcd .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.sort("dep_delay", descending=True).select( "month", "day", "carrier", "flight", "dep_delay" ).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 5)
monthdaycarrierflightdep_delay
i64i64stri64i64
11"EV"4308null
11"AA"791null
11"AA"1925null
``` ::: ::: With `nulls_last=True`, the first row is the 1,301-minute Honolulu flight from @sec-verb-topk. **Rule:** pass `nulls_last=True` to every `sort()` that feeds `head()`, a "first per group", or a report. ### Ties: unstable sorts, arbitrary `top_k()` {#sec-verb-ties} Number the rows, sort by day, and see where the file's first rows end up: ::: {#0def6574 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df_indexed = flights_df.with_row_index("row") by_day_default = flights_df_indexed.sort("month", "day") by_day_stable = flights_df_indexed.sort("month", "day", maintain_order=True) { "default: first rows": by_day_default["row"].head(5).to_list(), "maintain_order: first rows": by_day_stable["row"].head(5).to_list(), "rows in a different position": (by_day_default["row"] != by_day_stable["row"]).sum(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` {'default: first rows': [0, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'maintain_order: first rows': [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], 'rows in a different position': 228457} ``` ::: ::: Every row is in the right day either way, but the default sort reorders rows within a day: two thirds of all rows land somewhere other than where a stable sort puts them. The reordering was the same in every run here, and single-key sorts happened to be stable, but only `maintain_order=True` guarantees either. It matters as soon as the next step takes "the first row" of each day. `top_k()` has the same blind spot. 342 flights tie for the longest distance (JFK → HNL); `slice_max(distance, n = 3)` returns all of them. `top_k()` returns 3, and not the first 3 in the file: ::: {#f2effb70 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df_indexed.top_k(3, by="distance").select("row", "origin", "dest", "distance") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Keep the ties with a rank filter, or make the choice deterministic with a tie-breaker key (`reverse=` per key: largest distance, then smallest row number): ::: {#3b5b27a0 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} { "ties kept (slice_max)": flights_df.filter( pl.col("distance").rank("min", descending=True) <= 3 ).height, "first 3 in file order": flights_df_indexed.top_k( 3, by=["distance", "row"], reverse=[False, True] )["row"].to_list(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` {'ties kept (slice_max)': 342, 'first 3 in file order': [162, 1073, 2018]} ``` ::: ::: ### `unique()` defaults: any copy, any order {#sec-verb-unique-defaults} Without `maintain_order=True`, the row order of `unique()` is not just arbitrary, it changes from call to call: ::: {#18f75276 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} carrier_orders = {tuple(flights_df.unique(subset="carrier")["carrier"]) for _ in range(20)} len(carrier_orders) # distinct orderings in 20 identical calls ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` 20 ``` ::: ::: That breaks frozen renders, tests and diffs. The default `keep="any"` is the same kind of licence: in every probe on 2.0 it returned the first copy, but the docstring guarantees nothing. When the surviving row matters, spell out both: `unique(subset=..., keep="first", maintain_order=True)`. Per the docstring, `maintain_order=True` also keeps that step off the streaming engine. ### Selections don't deduplicate {#sec-verb-select-dupes} tidyselect combines selections as a **set**: `select(time_hour, everything())` names `time_hour` twice and keeps it once, which is the classic way to move a column to the front. A Polars `select()` is a **list** of expressions, and two outputs with the same name are an error: ::: {#9d9b32c0 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select("time_hour", pl.all()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
DuplicateError: projections contained duplicate output name 'time_hour'. It's possible that multiple expressions are returning the same default column name. If this is the case, try renaming the columns with `.alias("new_name")` to avoid duplicate column names.
``` ::: ::: ::: Exclude it from the rest instead: `select("time_hour", pl.exclude("time_hour"))`. Selector algebra does deduplicate, but a selector returns columns in **schema order**, so `select(cs.by_name("time_hour") | cs.all())` leaves `time_hour` last, where it was. ### Some column verbs work in place {#sec-verb-in-place} Almost every Polars method returns a new frame. Assigning to `df.columns` and calling `insert_column()` modify the frame itself instead, so every Python name bound to that frame sees the change: ::: {#4c69e95c .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} dates_df = flights_df.select("year", "month", "day").head(2) same_df = dates_df # a second name, not a copy dates_df.columns = ["yr", "mo", "dy"] # in place returned_df = dates_df.insert_column(0, pl.Series("id", [1, 2])) # in place, too same_df.columns, returned_df is dates_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` (['id', 'yr', 'mo', 'dy'], True) ``` ::: ::: R's `names(df) <- ...` is copy-on-modify: another variable bound to the old frame keeps the old names. `replace_column()` and `drop_in_place()` also work in place. `rename()`, `with_columns()` and `select()` never do. ## Recipes {#sec-verb-recipes} **Rows with the max per group, ties kept** (R4DS: `group_by(dest) |> slice_max(arr_delay, n = 1)`). Compare each row with its group's max: ::: {#9aabc089 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} worst_arrival_df = flights_df.filter( pl.col("arr_delay") == pl.col("arr_delay").max().over("dest") ) worst_arrival_df.height, worst_arrival_df["dest"].n_unique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ``` (107, 104) ``` ::: ::: R4DS gets 108 rows for 105 destinations. The extra one is the single flight to LGA, whose `arr_delay` is `NA`: with `na_rm = FALSE`, `slice_max()` returns `NA` rows when a group has nothing else. In Polars that group's max is null, the comparison is null, and `filter()` drops the row. **First and last flight of each day.** `datasets.flights()` is not in date order (the months run 1, 10, 11, 12, 2, …), so "first" needs an explicit sort. Drop cancelled flights, sort with `maintain_order=True` so equal departure times keep file order, then keep the first copy per day: ::: {#b151a1a9 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df_departed = flights_df.drop_nulls("dep_time").sort( "month", "day", "dep_time", maintain_order=True ) flights_df_departed.unique( subset=["month", "day"], keep="first", maintain_order=True ).select("month", "day", "dep_time", "carrier", "flight", "dest").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ```{=html}

Sort by time, then keep the last copy per key. Drop null keys first, because all nulls count as one key: ::: {#ea16fc25 .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.drop_nulls("tailnum").sort("time_hour", maintain_order=True).unique( subset="tailnum", keep="last", maintain_order=True ).select("tailnum", "time_hour", "origin", "dest").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ```{=html}

Build the name list in Python; `cs.expand_selector()` turns a selector into names, so tidyselect-style arguments work too: ::: {#5f63f96b .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} def relocate(df, columns, *, before=None, after=None): """Move `columns` (names or a selector) before/after an anchor column.""" if cs.is_selector(columns): columns = cs.expand_selector(df, columns) columns = [columns] if isinstance(columns, str) else list(columns) rest = [c for c in df.columns if c not in columns] if before is not None: at = rest.index(before) elif after is not None: at = rest.index(after) + 1 else: at = 0 return df.select(rest[:at] + columns + rest[at:]) relocate(flights_df, cs.starts_with("arr"), before="dep_time").columns[:7] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ``` ['year', 'month', 'day', 'arr_time', 'arr_delay', 'dep_time', 'sched_dep_time'] ``` ::: ::: ## See also {#sec-verb-see-also} - Cheatsheet: [Select Columns](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-select) · [Filter Rows](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-filter) · [Sort Rows](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-sort) · [Gotchas at a Glance](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-gotchas) - Before: [Expressions & Contexts](../core/expressions.qmd) (contexts, and why expression-level `sort()` misaligns rows) · [Selectors & Expression Expansion](../core/selectors.qmd) - Next: [Grouping & Aggregation](group-agg.qmd) · [Window Functions](window.qmd) · [Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd) - Polars API: [`DataFrame.unique`](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/dataframe/api/polars.DataFrame.unique.html) · [`DataFrame.sort`](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/dataframe/api/polars.DataFrame.sort.html) · [`DataFrame.top_k`](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/dataframe/api/polars.DataFrame.top_k.html) - R side: R4DS 2e, [Data transformation](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html);
